title: Bayesian Learning
oneLiner: Choose model parameters that make the data most likely, let prior beliefs pull them sensibly, and classify with Naïve Bayes.

what.html:
Bayesian learning treats a model's parameters as uncertain quantities and uses probability to learn them from data. Two recipes appear everywhere: maximum likelihood (MLE) picks the parameters that make the observed data most probable; maximum a posteriori (MAP) also weighs in what we believed before seeing the data (the prior).

Everyday versionA friend's coin lands heads 3 times out of 3. MLE says "this coin always lands heads". MAP says "most coins are fair, so it's probably a bit biased, not a trick coin". With 300 tosses, both would agree.

The same thinking gives the Naïve Bayes classifier: estimate how likely each feature value is in each class, multiply, and pick the class with the highest score.

why.html:
• It explains the loss functions you already use. Least squares is MLE under Gaussian noise; logistic regression's log-loss is MLE for yes/no outcomes; absolute error is MLE under Laplace noise.
  • Priors fight overfitting when data are scarce.
  • Naïve Bayes is fast, simple and strong for spam filtering, news categories, sentiment and other text tasks.
  • Beliefs update incrementally: today's posterior is tomorrow's prior.

how.title: A distribution is a model plus parameters
how.html: A normal distribution is described by θ = (mean, SD); a regression line by θ = (θ₀, θ₁, θ₂). Learning means estimating θ from data, assuming the samples are independent and identically distributed (IID).

how.title: MLE: make the data as likely as possible
how.html: Write the likelihood L(θ) = product of the probabilities of every observation. Take the log (products become sums), differentiate, set to zero, solve. In the session's discrete example, 10 observations give θ̂ = 0.5.

how.title: Why least squares is 'right'
how.html: If y = θᵀx + Gaussian noise, the log-likelihood is a constant minus ½Σ(y − θᵀx)²/σ². So maximising the likelihood is exactly minimising the sum of squared errors. If the noise is Laplace (heavier tails), MLE becomes minimising absolute errors instead.

how.title: Where logistic regression's cost comes from
how.html: Each label is a coin flip with P(y = 1) = σ(θᵀx). The log-likelihood is Σ[y log σ + (1 − y) log(1 − σ)], the negative of the cross-entropy cost, and its gradient is Σ(y − σ(θᵀx))x: the gradient-descent update from Module 4.

how.title: Bayes' theorem: update beliefs
how.html: posterior = likelihood × prior / evidence: P(θ | data) = P(data | θ)P(θ)/P(data). The prior is your belief before the data; the posterior is your belief after. With more data the likelihood dominates and the prior matters less.

how.title: MAP: the most probable parameters
how.html: MAP maximises likelihood × prior. Example: a prior 2x on [0, 1] and a likelihood x(1 − x)² (from observing y = 3) give a posterior ∝ 2x²(1 − x)², which peaks at x = 0.5. With a flat prior, MAP and MLE coincide.

how.title: Best prediction ≠ best single hypothesis
how.html: Three hypotheses with posteriors 0.4, 0.3, 0.3: the most probable one (h1) says "+", but the other two say "−". Weighting every hypothesis by its posterior (the Bayes optimal classifier) says "−" with 0.6. The cheaper Gibbs rule picks one hypothesis at random and is at most twice as wrong on average.

how.title: Naïve Bayes: assume features are independent given the class
how.html: Directly estimating P(all features | class) needs huge amounts of data. Naïve Bayes assumes each feature is independent of the others once you know the class, so P(x₁, …, xₙ | y) = Π P(xᵢ | y). Predict the class maximising P(y) × Π P(xᵢ | y); the denominator P(x) can be ignored.

how.title: Learning is counting
how.html: For categorical features, P(Sky = Sunny | Yes) is just "how many Yes days were Sunny / number of Yes days". For the session's new day (Sunny, Warm, Normal, Strong, Change): Yes scores 0.0635, No scores 0.0067 → EnjoySport = Yes.

how.title: Zero counts and Laplace smoothing
how.html: If "Rainy" never occurred on a Yes day, P(Rainy | Yes) = 0 and the whole product becomes 0, whatever the other features say. Laplace smoothing adds 1 to every count (and the number of possible values to the denominator), so nothing is ever exactly impossible. The second test day flips from No to Yes once smoothed.

how.title: Numbers instead of categories: Gaussian Naïve Bayes
how.html: For a numeric feature such as humidity or study hours, assume each class's values follow a normal curve: estimate its mean and spread, then use the bell-curve height at the new value as P(xᵢ | y).

how.title: Text: bag of words
how.html: Ignore word order; count words. P(word | class) = (count of that word in the class + 1) / (total words in the class + vocabulary size). "A very close game" scores 2.8 × 10⁻⁵ for Sports vs 5.7 × 10⁻⁶ for Not sports → Sports.

how.title: Naïve Bayes and logistic regression
how.html: Naïve Bayes is generative: it learns P(y) and P(x | y) and can even generate data. Logistic regression is discriminative: it learns P(y | x) directly. Gaussian Naïve Bayes implies exactly the logistic form for P(y | x), so they are close relatives that may still give different answers.

how.title: Strengths and practical issues
how.html: Each example nudges hypothesis probabilities up or down instead of eliminating hypotheses outright, and prior knowledge can be built in. But you need many probabilities to start with, and the full Bayes-optimal computation grows with the number of hypotheses.

demo.html: Pick a prior, then toss the coin. Watch three things: with very few tosses MAP stays near the prior while MLE jumps to extremes (e.g. 1.0 after one head); with "Random ×10" pressed a few times both converge to the true θ; a strong prior (Beta(5, 5)) takes more data to move.

example.html:
Applications: categorising news, email spam detection, face recognition, sentiment analysis, and handwritten digit recognition (black/white pixels → is it a 5 or a 6?).

Students' results. Classify a male student with 3.5 study hours as Pass or Fail by combining a categorical feature (gender) with a Gaussian feature (hours): the answer is Fail.

Supplementary In telecom customer care, Naïve Bayes on ticket text (words like "no signal", "bill", "recharge") routes complaints to the right team in milliseconds.

misunderstandings: MLE and MAP always give different answers.
With a uniform prior they are identical; with lots of data they converge.
Naïve Bayes needs the features to really be independent.
The assumption is usually false, yet the classifier often still ranks classes well; its probabilities, however, tend to be over-confident.
A zero count just means a small probability.
Without smoothing, one zero makes the whole product zero and silently decides the class.
The most probable hypothesis gives the most probable prediction.
Combining all hypotheses weighted by posterior (Bayes optimal) can disagree with the single MAP hypothesis.
takeaways: MLE chooses θ that maximises the (log-)likelihood of IID data: log, differentiate, solve.
Gaussian noise → least squares; Bernoulli labels → logistic log-loss; Laplace noise → absolute error.
MAP maximises likelihood × prior; equals MLE under a uniform prior.
Bayes optimal classification averages predictions over hypotheses weighted by posterior; Gibbs samples one.
Naïve Bayes: argmax P(y)ΠP(xᵢ|y), with counts (Laplace-smoothed), Gaussians for numbers, word counts for text.
thirty: Bayesian learning estimates model parameters with probability. Maximum likelihood picks the parameters that make the observed IID data most probable: write the log-likelihood, differentiate and solve. Under Gaussian noise that gives least squares, and for binary labels the logistic regression cost. MAP also multiplies by a prior and picks the most probable parameters, matching MLE when the prior is flat. For prediction, the Bayes optimal classifier averages all hypotheses by posterior weight. Naïve Bayes assumes features are independent given the class, so it multiplies per-feature probabilities, with Laplace smoothing for zero counts and Gaussians for numeric features.
